summary: This is the introduction to William Vincent's book 'Django for Beginners', a project-based beginner tutorial for the Django 4.2 web framework and Python 3.11. It explains that the book builds five progressively complex apps (Hello World, Pages, Message Board, Blog, Newspaper) and covers Django's history, its batteries-included philosophy compared with Flask, the Django 4.2 LTS release and its async progress, the 17-chapter structure, code conventions, advice on getting unstuck, and the Django community.
one_line: Introduction to William Vincent's beginner-friendly book teaching Django 4.2 and Python 3.11 through five project-based web apps.
key_facts: Django for Beginners is written for Django 4.2 and Python 3.11.
The book builds five progressively more complex web applications: Hello, World; Pages; Message Board; Blog; and Newspaper.
Websites named as using Django include Instagram, Pinterest, Bitbucket, and Disqus.
Django 4.2 was released in April 2023 and has official support for Python 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, and 3.11.
Django 4.2 is an LTS (Long Term Support) release that will receive security updates for at least three years after its release.
Django 3.2 is the previous LTS release, and its support ends in April 2024.
Django 3.0 added ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface).
Django's release schedule includes monthly security/bug fixes and a major new release every eight months.
The author wrote the book because Django has incredible documentation but needs more beginner-friendly tutorials.
Flask is described as a microframework that provides only the bare minimum and requires adding a dozen or more third-party packages.
Django adopts an MVT (Model-View-Template) approach, slightly different from the dominant MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern.
Chapter 3 introduces templates and class-based views and deploys the Pages app to Fly.io.
Chapter 4 builds a Message Board app and Chapter 5 deploys it.
Chapter 10 covers a custom user model, which the author calls a Django best practice rarely addressed in tutorials.
The Conclusion is followed by a note that the next chapter is Chapter 1: Initial Set Up.
